stories.title: Islam's first century
stories.region: Arabia to Spain and Central Asia
stories.blurb: How did a religious movement in a small Arabian town become an empire stretching from Spain to Central Asia within about 120 years?

steps.name: Muhammad's first revelation
steps.what: Muhammad, a Meccan merchant of the Quraysh tribe, reported his first revelation while in retreat in a cave on Jabal al-Nour.
steps.why: Muslim tradition dates the start of the Quran and of Islam to this moment.

steps.name: Hijrah
steps.what: Facing hostility in Mecca, Muhammad and his followers migrated about 340 km north to Yathrib, later called Medina.
steps.why: In Medina Muhammad led a community with its own laws and army, and the year of the migration became year 1 of the Islamic calendar.

steps.name: Conquest of Mecca
steps.what: Muhammad entered Mecca with an army of about 10,000 almost without fighting and cleared the idols from the Kaaba.
steps.why: Taking Arabia's main shrine and trading town brought most Arabian tribes to submit within two years.

steps.name: Death of Muhammad
steps.what: Muhammad died in Medina and Abu Bakr was chosen as the first caliph, or successor, as political leader of the community.
steps.why: The question of who should lead after Muhammad, settled this way, later divided Sunni and Shia Muslims.

steps.name: Battle of al-Qadisiyyah
steps.what: An Arab army under Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas defeated the Sasanian Persian army, whose commander Rostam Farrokhzad was killed.
steps.why: It opened Iraq, the richest province of the Persian Empire, and led to the fall of the Sasanian capital Ctesiphon.

steps.name: Battle of the Yarmuk
steps.what: Over six days an Arab army defeated a much larger Byzantine army near the Yarmouk river, a tributary of the Jordan.
steps.why: The Byzantines abandoned Syria, and Damascus and Jerusalem passed to Arab rule.

steps.name: Arab conquest of Egypt
steps.what: Amr ibn al-As besieged Alexandria and the Byzantines agreed by treaty to evacuate the city, which they left in 642.
steps.why: Egypt's grain and taxes, once feeding Constantinople, now went to the caliphate.

steps.name: History of the Quran
steps.what: The third caliph Uthman had a standard written text of the Quran compiled and copies sent to the main garrison cities, ordering other versions burned.
steps.why: A single authorised text helped hold together a community now spread over three continents.

steps.name: Battle of Karbala
steps.what: Husayn, grandson of Muhammad, and about 70 companions were killed by an army sent by the Umayyad caliph Yazid I.
steps.why: Husayn's death became the central event of Shia memory and deepened the split over leadership of the community.

steps.name: Dome of the Rock
steps.what: The Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik completed the Dome of the Rock on the Temple Mount, with Quranic inscriptions in its mosaics.
steps.why: It is the oldest surviving major Islamic monument and announced the new faith in a city holy to Jews and Christians.

steps.name: Umayyad Mosque
steps.what: Caliph al-Walid I began building the Great Mosque of Damascus on the site of a Christian basilica, decorated with gold mosaics by Byzantine craftsmen.
steps.why: Damascus was the capital of the Umayyad empire, and the mosque became a model for mosques across the Islamic world.

steps.name: Battle of Guadalete
steps.what: Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed from North Africa with mostly Berber troops and defeated the Visigothic king Roderic, who disappeared in the battle.
steps.why: Within a few years most of the Iberian Peninsula became al-Andalus, part of the caliphate.

steps.name: Battle of Tours
who: Abd al-Rahman ibn Abd Allah al-Ghafiqi
steps.what: A Frankish army under Charles Martel defeated an Umayyad raiding army, whose governor Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi was killed.
steps.why: It marked roughly the northern limit of Umayyad raids into Francia.

steps.name: Abbasid revolution
steps.what: Abu Muslim raised the black banners of the Abbasid cause in Khorasan near Merv, drawing on Persian converts and Arab settlers unhappy with Umayyad rule.
steps.why: The revolt turned resentment at Umayyad favouritism toward Arab elites into a movement that toppled the dynasty.

steps.name: Battle of the Zab
steps.what: Abbasid forces under Abdallah ibn Ali defeated the last Umayyad caliph Marwan II, who fled to Egypt and was killed later that year.
steps.why: The Abbasids took the caliphate and moved its centre from Syria to Iraq.

steps.name: Battle of Talas
steps.what: An Abbasid army, helped by the defection of Karluk Turks, defeated a Tang Chinese army under Gao Xianzhi near the Talas river.
steps.why: It marked the meeting point of the caliphate and Tang China in Central Asia, and Tang power there soon declined.

stories.title: Tang China, glory to collapse
stories.blurb: How did the Tang dynasty build one of the most open and powerful states in the world, and why did it break apart after An Lushan's rebellion?

steps.name: Founding of the Tang dynasty
steps.what: Li Yuan, a Sui general who had taken Chang'an, declared himself emperor of a new Tang dynasty as the Sui collapsed.
steps.why: Chang'an became the capital of a dynasty that lasted almost three centuries.

steps.name: Xuanwu Gate Incident
steps.what: Li Shimin ambushed and killed his brothers, the crown prince Li Jiancheng and Li Yuanji, at the palace's Xuanwu Gate, and his father soon abdicated.
steps.why: Li Shimin, as Emperor Taizong, built the strong early Tang state and its westward expansion.

steps.name: Journey of Xuanzang
steps.what: The Buddhist monk Xuanzang left Chang'an without imperial permission to travel west in search of Buddhist texts.
steps.why: His 16-year journey along the Silk Road tied Tang China to Central Asia and India.

steps.name: Xuanzang at Nalanda
steps.what: Xuanzang reached the great Buddhist monastery of Nalanda in north India and studied there for several years under the abbot Silabhadra.
steps.why: Nalanda was the leading centre of Buddhist learning, and the texts he gathered shaped Chinese Buddhism.

steps.name: Return of Xuanzang
steps.what: Xuanzang returned to Chang'an with 657 Buddhist texts, was received by Emperor Taizong, and spent the rest of his life translating them.
steps.why: His travel record, the Great Tang Records on the Western Regions, is a key source for 7th century Central Asia and India.

steps.name: Wu Zetian
steps.what: Wu Zetian, widow of Emperor Gaozong, declared herself emperor of a new Zhou dynasty, ruling mostly from Luoyang until 705.
steps.why: She was the only woman to rule China as emperor in her own name, and widened recruitment of officials through the examinations.

steps.name: Li Bai at the Tang court
steps.what: The poet Li Bai was summoned to Chang'an and served at Emperor Xuanzong's court for about two years.
steps.why: Xuanzong's reign was the high point of Tang culture, the age of Li Bai and Du Fu.

steps.name: Battle of Talas
steps.what: A Tang army under the Korean-born general Gao Xianzhi was defeated by Abbasid forces near the Talas river after Karluk Turks changed sides.
steps.why: It was the furthest west Tang armies fought, and Tang withdrawal from Central Asia followed the crisis of 755.

steps.name: An Lushan rebellion
steps.what: An Lushan, a frontier general commanding about 150,000 troops in the northeast, rebelled and marched south, taking Luoyang within weeks.
steps.why: The eight-year war devastated north China and permanently weakened the central government.

steps.name: Death of Yang Guifei
steps.what: As Xuanzong fled Chang'an toward Sichuan, his guards mutinied at Mawei and forced him to have his consort Yang Guifei killed.
steps.why: Xuanzong abdicated soon after, and the story became a symbol of the dynasty's fall from glory.

steps.name: Siege of Suiyang
steps.what: Zhang Xun's small garrison held Suiyang for about ten months against rebel armies, until starvation forced its fall.
steps.why: The defence kept rebels out of the Huai and Yangtze valleys, whose taxes kept the Tang alive.

steps.name: Huichang persecution of Buddhism
steps.what: Emperor Wuzong ordered thousands of Buddhist monasteries closed and about 260,000 monks and nuns returned to lay life, seizing their land and bronze.
steps.why: A cash-hungry state turned on the wealth of Buddhist institutions, ending the most open phase of Tang religious life.

steps.name: Diamond Sutra
steps.what: A woodblock-printed copy of the Diamond Sutra was made, later found sealed in a cave at Dunhuang.
steps.why: It is the oldest dated printed book known, showing that printing was in everyday use by late Tang.

steps.name: Guangzhou massacre
steps.what: Rebels under Huang Chao sacked Guangzhou, killing many of its foreign Muslim, Jewish, Christian and Zoroastrian merchants.
steps.why: The rebellion, begun among salt smugglers in 874-875, now reached China's main overseas trading port.

steps.date_note: entered the city at the turn of 880-881
steps.name: Huang Chao takes Chang'an
steps.what: Huang Chao's army entered Chang'an, Emperor Xizong fled to Sichuan, and Huang declared himself emperor of a new state.
steps.why: Although the rebels were driven out in 883, the court now depended on regional warlords.

steps.name: End of the Tang dynasty
steps.what: The warlord Zhu Wen, a former follower of Huang Chao, forced the last Tang emperor to abdicate and founded the Later Liang dynasty at Kaifeng.
steps.why: China split into the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms until the Song reunified it.

stories.title: Baghdad and the House of Wisdom
stories.blurb: How did Baghdad become the richest city and greatest centre of learning in the medieval world, and what ended its golden age?

steps.name: Founding of Baghdad
steps.what: The Abbasid caliph al-Mansur laid out a new capital on the Tigris as a round walled city about 2 km across, with four gates.
steps.why: The site sat where the Tigris came closest to the Euphrates, on canal and caravan routes linking the Gulf, Iran and Syria.

steps.name: Paper mills in Baghdad
steps.what: Baghdad's first paper mill is reported in the time of Harun al-Rashid, using a craft learned from Chinese papermakers in Central Asia.
steps.why: Cheap paper replaced papyrus and parchment, and made a large book trade and government archive possible.

steps.name: Fourth Fitna
steps.what: In a civil war between Harun's sons, al-Ma'mun's general Tahir besieged Baghdad for about a year, and al-Amin was killed after the city fell.
steps.why: Much of the city was damaged, and al-Ma'mun emerged as caliph.

steps.name: Al-Jabr
steps.what: Al-Khwarizmi, a scholar at al-Ma'mun's court, wrote a book on solving equations by completion and balancing, dedicated to the caliph.
steps.why: Its title gave the world the word algebra, and his name gave the word algorithm.

steps.name: House of Wisdom
steps.what: Under al-Ma'mun the House of Wisdom became a library and centre where scholars translated Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic.
steps.why: Translated Aristotle, Galen, Euclid and Ptolemy became the base of a new Arabic science later passed on to Europe.

steps.name: Samarra
steps.what: Caliph al-Mu'tasim moved the capital about 125 km up the Tigris to a new city at Samarra, partly to separate his Turkish soldiers from Baghdad's people.
steps.why: Reliance on Turkish slave soldiers gave military commanders growing power over the caliphs.

steps.name: Zanj Rebellion
steps.what: Enslaved East Africans forced to clear salt flats near Basra rose under Ali ibn Muhammad and held southern Iraq for 14 years, sacking Basra in 871.
steps.why: The revolt drained Abbasid resources and showed the human cost of the plantation economy feeding the cities.

steps.name: Journey of Ahmad ibn Fadlan
steps.what: Ibn Fadlan left Baghdad as secretary of a caliphal embassy to the king of the Volga Bulgars.
steps.why: His report is one of the few eyewitness accounts of northern peoples, including the Rus, written by a Baghdad official.

steps.name: Execution of al-Hallaj
steps.what: The Sufi mystic al-Hallaj, accused of heresy for saying 'I am the Truth', was publicly executed in Baghdad after a long trial.
steps.why: His death showed the tensions between mystics, jurists and the court in the caliphal capital.

steps.name: Ibn Fadlan on the Volga
steps.what: After crossing Iran, Khwarazm and the steppe, the embassy reached the Volga Bulgar king, who had asked for help building a mosque and fort.
steps.why: It shows how far Baghdad's influence and trade networks reached by the 10th century.

steps.name: Buyid dynasty
steps.what: The Buyid prince Ahmad, given the title Mu'izz al-Dawla, entered Baghdad and took real power, leaving the caliph a religious figurehead.
steps.why: From now on the caliphs reigned but did not rule.

steps.name: Tughril enters Baghdad
steps.what: The Seljuk Turkish leader Tughril entered Baghdad, ended Buyid rule, and was named sultan by the caliph.
steps.why: Sunni Turkish sultans now protected the caliphate and ruled the Middle East.

steps.name: Nizamiyya of Baghdad
steps.what: The Seljuk vizier Nizam al-Mulk opened a large madrasa in Baghdad where students were taught law with salaries and lodging paid by an endowment.
steps.why: It became a model for state-supported Sunni colleges across the Islamic world; al-Ghazali later taught there.

steps.name: Siege of Alamut
steps.what: Hulagu Khan's Mongol army forced the surrender of the Nizari Ismaili leader and took the mountain fortresses of northern Iran, including Alamut.
steps.why: With Iran secured, the Mongols turned on Baghdad.

steps.name: Siege of Baghdad
steps.what: After a two-week siege the Mongols took Baghdad, killed the caliph al-Musta'sim and many thousands of inhabitants, and destroyed libraries.
steps.why: It ended the Abbasid caliphate in Baghdad and is often taken as the end of the city's golden age.

stories.title: The Viking age
stories.blurb: How did seafarers from Scandinavia go from raiding monasteries to settling, trading and ruling from Newfoundland to Kiev?

steps.name: Raid on Lindisfarne
steps.what: Norse raiders sacked the monastery on Lindisfarne off Northumbria, killing monks and taking treasure; Alcuin wrote of the shock from Charlemagne's court.
steps.why: It is the conventional start of the Viking age in western Europe.

steps.name: Siege of Paris (845)
steps.what: A Viking fleet of about 120 ships sailed up the Seine and took Paris; Charles the Bald paid 7,000 pounds of silver to make them leave.
steps.why: Paying tribute showed raiders that river towns in Francia were rich and poorly defended.

steps.name: Siege of Constantinople (860)
steps.what: A Rus fleet of about 200 ships raided the suburbs of Constantinople while the emperor was away; Patriarch Photios preached about the attack.
steps.why: It was the first recorded Rus attack on the Byzantine capital, reached by rivers from the Baltic to the Black Sea.

steps.date_note: traditional date from the Primary Chronicle
steps.name: Rurik at Novgorod
steps.what: According to the Primary Chronicle, the Varangian Rurik was invited to rule the tribes around Novgorod.
steps.why: His dynasty, the Rurikids, ruled Rus and later Muscovy until 1598.

steps.name: Great Heathen Army takes York
steps.what: The Great Heathen Army, which had landed in East Anglia in 865, captured York, the chief town of Northumbria.
steps.why: Raiding turned into conquest, and York became the centre of a Viking kingdom.

steps.name: Settlement of Iceland
steps.what: Ingólfr Arnarson is said to have settled at Reykjavik, the first of thousands of Norse farmers who claimed Iceland's coastal land over 60 years.
steps.why: Iceland showed Norse expansion as farming migration, not only raiding.

steps.name: Battle of Edington
steps.what: Alfred of Wessex defeated the Danish leader Guthrum, who then accepted baptism and withdrew to East Anglia.
steps.why: England was divided between Wessex and the Danelaw, where Scandinavian law and place names took root.

steps.name: Oleg takes Kiev
steps.what: According to the Primary Chronicle, Oleg of Novgorod took Kiev and made it the centre of the Rus state on the Dnieper route.
steps.why: Kiev controlled the river trade with Byzantium, the source of Rus wealth.

steps.name: Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte
steps.what: Charles the Simple granted the Viking leader Rollo land around Rouen in return for defending the lower Seine against other raiders.
steps.why: Rollo's land grew into the Duchy of Normandy, whose Normans later conquered England.

steps.name: Althing
steps.what: Icelanders founded the Althing, a yearly open-air assembly at Thingvellir where chieftains made laws and settled disputes.
steps.why: A society without a king governed itself through law and assembly.

steps.name: Hedeby
steps.what: The traveller Ibrahim ibn Yaqub described Hedeby, a Danish trading town where goods from the Baltic, Francia and the Islamic world changed hands.
steps.why: Towns like Hedeby show the Viking age as an age of trade, using silver coins from as far as Baghdad.

steps.name: Erik the Red in Greenland
steps.what: Erik the Red, exiled from Iceland, led settlers in about 14 ships to southwest Greenland and farmed at Brattahlíð.
steps.why: The Greenland colony was the base for voyages further west and lasted about 450 years.

steps.name: Christianization of Kievan Rus'
steps.what: Grand Prince Vladimir accepted Byzantine Orthodox Christianity, married the emperor's sister Anna, and had the people of Kiev baptised in the Dnieper.
steps.why: Rus turned toward Byzantium for its religion, script and art.

steps.name: Battle of Assandun
steps.what: Cnut defeated Edmund Ironside; after Edmund died that November, Cnut became king of all England.
steps.why: Cnut later ruled England, Denmark and Norway, a North Sea empire.

steps.name: L'Anse aux Meadows
steps.what: Norse visitors cut wood with metal tools at this site in Newfoundland, dated by tree rings to 1021; the sagas tell of Leif Erikson's voyage to Vinland around 1000.
steps.why: It is the only confirmed Norse site in the Americas, about 500 years before Columbus.

steps.name: Battle of Stamford Bridge
steps.what: Harold Godwinson of England defeated and killed the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada, who had invaded with about 300 ships.
steps.why: It is often taken as the end of the Viking age; three weeks later Harold lost to William of Normandy at Hastings.

stories.title: Charlemagne's Europe
stories.blurb: How did Charlemagne unite most of western Christian Europe into one empire, and why did his grandsons divide it within 30 years of his death?

steps.name: Charlemagne becomes king
steps.what: After the death of their father Pepin the Short, Charlemagne was crowned king of the Franks at Noyon, sharing the kingdom with his brother Carloman.
steps.why: Carloman's death in 771 left Charlemagne sole ruler of the Franks.

steps.name: Saxon Wars
steps.what: Charlemagne took the Saxon fort of Eresburg and destroyed the Irminsul, a sacred pillar of the pagan Saxons.
steps.why: This began 30 years of war that forced the Saxons into the Frankish kingdom and the Christian church.

steps.name: Siege of Pavia
steps.what: After a siege of about nine months, Pavia surrendered and the Lombard king Desiderius was sent to a monastery; Charlemagne took the title King of the Lombards.
steps.why: Northern Italy joined the Frankish realm and Charlemagne became protector of the pope.

steps.name: Battle of Roncevaux Pass
steps.what: Returning from a campaign in Spain, the Frankish rearguard was ambushed and destroyed by Basques in the Pyrenees, and the commander Roland was killed.
steps.why: It set limits on expansion into Spain and later inspired the Song of Roland.

steps.name: Massacre of Verden
steps.what: After a Saxon revolt, Charlemagne had about 4,500 Saxon prisoners executed at Verden, according to the Royal Frankish Annals.
steps.why: It shows the brutality of the forced conversion of Saxony.

steps.name: Admonitio generalis
steps.what: Charlemagne issued a long set of instructions on church reform, ordering that every monastery and cathedral have a school to teach boys reading.
steps.why: With scholars like Alcuin, this drove the Carolingian Renaissance, which copied and preserved much of Latin literature.

steps.name: Fossa Carolina
steps.what: Charlemagne had thousands of workers dig a canal to link the Rhine and Danube river systems.
steps.why: It was the largest engineering project of the age, though it was probably never fully usable.

steps.name: Coronation of Charlemagne
steps.what: At Christmas mass in St Peter's, Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor of the Romans.
steps.why: A western emperor existed again for the first time since 476, challenging Byzantium's claim.

steps.name: Abul-Abbas
steps.what: An Asian elephant named Abul-Abbas, a gift from the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid, arrived at Aachen with the envoy Isaac the Jew.
steps.why: Gift exchange with Baghdad shows Charlemagne's reach as a ruler known across the Mediterranean.

steps.name: Palatine Chapel at Aachen
steps.what: The octagonal Palatine Chapel at Aachen, modelled on churches in Ravenna and built with columns brought from Italy, was consecrated.
steps.why: Aachen became the court's settled centre and Charlemagne was buried in the chapel.

steps.name: Divisio Regnorum
steps.what: At Thionville Charlemagne set out a plan to divide the empire between his three sons after his death, following Frankish custom.
steps.why: Two of the sons died before him, so in the end the whole empire passed to Louis.

steps.name: Death of Charlemagne
steps.what: Charlemagne died at Aachen aged about 65 and was succeeded by his son Louis the Pious.
steps.why: The empire's unity now depended on Louis and the rules of inheritance.

steps.name: Ordinatio imperii
steps.what: Louis the Pious decreed that his eldest son Lothair would inherit the imperial title and authority over his brothers' kingdoms.
steps.why: Later changes to the plan for a fourth son, Charles, sparked civil wars between Louis and his sons.

steps.name: Battle of Fontenoy (841)
steps.what: Louis the German and Charles the Bald defeated their brother Lothair in one of the bloodiest battles among the Franks.
steps.why: It decided that the empire would be divided, not ruled by Lothair alone.

steps.name: Oaths of Strasbourg
steps.what: Louis and Charles swore alliance against Lothair, each in the language of the other's troops, an early Romance and an Old High German text.
steps.why: The oaths are among the earliest written records of French and German as separate languages.

steps.name: Treaty of Verdun
steps.what: The three grandsons divided the empire into West Francia, East Francia and a middle kingdom from the Low Countries to Italy.
steps.why: The division roughly outlined the later France and Germany, with a contested borderland between them.

stories.title: The Crusades
stories.blurb: Why did western Europeans fight for two centuries to hold the Holy Land, and how did those wars change Europe, Byzantium and the Islamic world?

steps.name: Council of Clermont
steps.what: Pope Urban II called on knights to march east to help Byzantium against the Seljuk Turks and to free Jerusalem, promising remission of sins.
steps.why: The speech launched the First Crusade and a new idea of holy war as penance.

steps.name: Rhineland massacres
steps.what: Bands of crusaders led by Count Emicho attacked Jewish communities in Speyer, Worms and Mainz, killing hundreds who refused baptism.
steps.why: Crusading zeal turned first on Jews at home, a pattern repeated in later crusades.

steps.name: Siege of Nicaea
steps.what: Crusader armies and Byzantine forces besieged the Seljuk capital Nicaea, which surrendered to the Byzantines in June.
steps.why: Cooperation with Byzantium began well but tensions over who would hold conquests grew.

steps.name: Siege of Antioch
steps.what: After an eight-month siege, a traitor let Bohemond's men into Antioch; the crusaders then beat off a relief army under Kerbogha.
steps.why: Bohemond kept the city for himself, founding the Principality of Antioch against his oath to Byzantium.

steps.name: Siege of Jerusalem (1099)
steps.what: Crusaders stormed Jerusalem after a five-week siege and massacred many of its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants.
steps.why: The Kingdom of Jerusalem and three other crusader states were set up along the Levant coast.

steps.name: Knights Templar
steps.what: Hugues de Payens and a few knights formed a religious order to protect pilgrims, housed in the Al-Aqsa Mosque on the Temple Mount.
steps.why: The military orders became the standing armies of the crusader states and powerful bankers across Europe.

steps.name: Krak des Chevaliers
steps.what: The castle was given to the Knights Hospitaller, who rebuilt it into one of the largest crusader fortresses, guarding the Homs gap.
steps.why: A few thousand settlers held a long coast against larger Muslim states largely through castles.

steps.name: Siege of Edessa (1144)
steps.what: Zengi, atabeg of Mosul and Aleppo, took Edessa after a four-week siege, ending the first crusader state.
steps.why: Its fall prompted the Second Crusade, which failed before Damascus in 1148.

steps.name: Battle of Hattin
steps.what: Saladin's army trapped the thirsty crusader army near the Sea of Galilee and destroyed it, capturing King Guy of Jerusalem.
steps.why: The kingdom lost almost all its field army and most of its towns within months.

steps.name: Siege of Jerusalem (1187)
steps.what: Balian of Ibelin surrendered Jerusalem to Saladin, who let most inhabitants leave on payment of ransom.
steps.why: Losing Jerusalem led to the Third Crusade.

steps.name: Siege of Acre (1189–1191)
steps.what: Crusaders besieged Acre for almost two years until Richard I and Philip II arrived and forced its surrender.
steps.why: Acre became the new capital of a smaller crusader kingdom.

steps.name: Treaty of Jaffa (1192)
steps.what: Richard and Saladin agreed a three-year truce: crusaders kept the coast from Tyre to Jaffa and Christian pilgrims could visit Jerusalem.
steps.why: The crusader states survived as a coastal strip dependent on trade and truces.

steps.name: Sack of Constantinople
steps.what: Fourth Crusade armies, in debt to Venice and drawn into Byzantine politics, stormed and plundered Constantinople for three days.
steps.why: Christians sacking the greatest Christian city crippled Byzantium and deepened the split between the Latin and Greek churches.

steps.name: Sixth Crusade
steps.what: Emperor Frederick II, under excommunication, gained Jerusalem by a ten-year treaty with Sultan al-Kamil of Egypt without a battle.
steps.why: Diplomacy achieved what armies had not, but angered hardliners on both sides.

steps.name: Battle of Mansurah
steps.what: Louis IX's invasion of Egypt stalled at Mansurah, and in April his army was defeated and he was captured and ransomed.
steps.why: The failure helped bring Mamluk soldiers to power in Egypt, the crusaders' most dangerous enemy.

steps.name: Siege of Acre (1291)
steps.what: The Mamluk sultan al-Ashraf Khalil besieged Acre with a large army and siege engines and stormed it after six weeks.
steps.why: The last crusader towns on the mainland fell within months, ending the crusader states.

stories.title: Song China's commercial revolution
stories.blurb: How did Song China become the world's most commercial and technologically advanced economy, with paper money, printing and gunpowder, and how was it conquered?

steps.name: Chenqiao mutiny
steps.what: Troops at Chenqiao proclaimed their general Zhao Kuangyin emperor; he took Kaifeng and founded the Song dynasty.
steps.why: Taizu then sidelined powerful generals in favour of civil officials chosen by examination.

steps.name: Chanyuan Treaty
steps.what: After a Liao invasion stalled at Chanyuan, the Song agreed to pay the Khitan Liao 100,000 taels of silver and 200,000 bolts of silk a year for peace.
steps.why: Peace on the northern frontier lasted over a century, letting trade and cities grow.

steps.name: Jiaozi (currency)
steps.what: The Song government took over the paper notes that Sichuan merchants had issued in place of heavy iron coins, creating official paper money.
steps.why: It was the first government-issued paper currency in the world.

steps.name: Wujing Zongyao
steps.what: A military manual compiled for the court gave the earliest known written formulas for gunpowder, for use in fire arrows and bombs.
steps.why: Gunpowder weapons, first used by Song armies, later spread across Eurasia.

steps.name: Wang Anshi's New Policies
steps.what: Chief minister Wang Anshi began reforms including state loans to farmers, a land survey and taxes paid in cash instead of labour.
steps.why: The reforms tried to harness a commercial economy for the state and split officials into bitter factions.

steps.name: Dream Pool Essays
steps.what: In retirement at his garden in Zhenjiang, Shen Kuo wrote notes describing Bi Sheng's movable type and the magnetic needle compass, among much else.
steps.why: It is the earliest description of movable type printing and of the compass used for direction.

steps.name: Along the River During the Qingming Festival
steps.what: Zhang Zeduan painted a five-metre scroll of daily life along a river near Kaifeng, with shops, inns, boats and hundreds of people.
steps.why: It shows the busy commercial city of perhaps a million people that Kaifeng had become.
steps.wikipedia: Along the River During the Qingming Festival

steps.date_note: city fell January 1127, captives taken north in spring
steps.name: Jingkang incident
steps.what: Jurchen Jin armies took Kaifeng and carried off the retired emperor Huizong, Emperor Qinzong and thousands of courtiers to the north.
steps.why: North China was lost, and the court rebuilt in the south as the Southern Song.

steps.name: Hangzhou becomes capital
steps.what: Emperor Gaozong settled the court at Hangzhou, then called Lin'an.
steps.why: Hangzhou grew into perhaps the largest city in the world, later described by Marco Polo.

steps.name: Treaty of Shaoxing
steps.what: The Song accepted the Huai River as the border and paid yearly tribute to the Jin; the general Yue Fei, who opposed peace, was executed in prison.
steps.why: The split of China into a Jurchen north and Song south was fixed for a century.

steps.name: Battle of Caishi
steps.what: A Song fleet with paddle-wheel ships and gunpowder bombs stopped a Jin army crossing the Yangtze.
steps.why: The navy and the river protected the southern economy from northern armies.

steps.name: Zhu Fan Zhi
steps.what: Zhao Rukuo (Zhao Rugua), maritime trade official at Quanzhou, wrote a guide to foreign lands and goods from Japan to East Africa.
steps.why: Quanzhou's sea trade in porcelain, silk and spices made the Song state rely on customs revenue.

steps.name: Battle of Xiangyang
steps.what: Mongol armies besieged the twin cities of Xiangyang and Fancheng for five years, finally using counterweight trebuchets built by Persian engineers.
steps.why: Its fall opened the Han River route into the Song heartland.

steps.name: Fall of Lin'an
steps.what: The Song regents surrendered Hangzhou and the child emperor to the Mongol general Bayan without a battle.
steps.why: The capital's peaceful surrender spared the city, but loyalists fled south with two young princes.
steps.wikipedia: Mongol conquest of the Song dynasty

steps.name: Battle of Yamen
steps.what: The Yuan fleet destroyed the last Song fleet; minister Lu Xiufu jumped into the sea holding the boy emperor Zhao Bing.
steps.why: It ended the Song dynasty, and all China came under Mongol rule.

stories.title: The classic Maya collapse
stories.blurb: Why were the great southern Maya cities, from Tikal to Copan, abandoned between about 800 and 950, while Chichen Itza in the north rose?

steps.date_note: 29 July 615 in the usual (GMT) calendar correlation
steps.name: Pakal becomes king of Palenque
steps.what: Pakal took the throne of Palenque aged 12 and ruled for 68 years.
steps.why: Palenque became one of the great western Maya cities during the classic peak.

steps.name: Calakmul attacks Tikal
steps.what: Yuknoom Ch'een II of Calakmul, the Snake (Kaan) kingdom, attacked Tikal and drove its king Nuun Ujol Chaak into exile.
steps.why: Calakmul and Tikal led rival alliances whose wars shaped the classic period.

steps.name: Temple of the Inscriptions
steps.what: Pakal died and was buried in a carved stone sarcophagus inside the Temple of the Inscriptions, whose panels record Palenque's dynastic history.
steps.why: Monumental tombs and long inscriptions show the wealth and labour classic kings commanded.

steps.name: Tikal defeats Calakmul
steps.what: Jasaw Chan K'awiil I of Tikal defeated Calakmul's king Yich'aak K'ak' and celebrated the victory on carved lintels.
steps.why: Tikal's revival weakened Calakmul's hegemony over the lowlands.

steps.name: Tikal Temple I
steps.what: A 47-metre pyramid temple was completed over the tomb of Jasaw Chan K'awiil I on Tikal's Great Plaza.
steps.why: Tikal was at its height, perhaps with tens of thousands of people around its centre.

steps.name: Quiriguá captures Copán's king
steps.what: K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat of Quirigua, once a subordinate of Copan, captured and beheaded Copan's king Uaxaclajuun Ub'aah K'awiil.
steps.why: A small vassal humiliating a great city shows how unstable Maya political networks were.

steps.name: Hieroglyphic Stairway of Copán
steps.what: Copan's king dedicated a stairway of about 2,200 glyphs telling the royal history of the city.
steps.why: It is the longest known Maya inscription, built to restore royal prestige after the 738 defeat.

steps.name: Fall of Dos Pilas
steps.what: Dos Pilas, capital of the Petexbatún kingdom, was defeated by former vassals and abandoned, and the region fell into constant warfare.
steps.why: The Petexbatún was one of the first areas to collapse, with walls built even across plazas.

steps.name: Bonampak murals
steps.what: Painters covered three rooms at Bonampak with murals of a royal court, a battle and the torture of captives.
steps.why: The murals show a warrior elite at its height only a few decades before the region was abandoned.

steps.name: Cancuén massacre
steps.what: About 31 members of Cancuen's royal court were killed and thrown into a palace pool, and the trading city was abandoned soon after.
steps.why: Sudden violent ends like this mark the collapse in the southern lowlands.

steps.name: Drought in the Maya lowlands
steps.what: Sediment cores from Lake Chichancanab and other lakes show a series of severe droughts in the 9th and 10th centuries.
steps.why: Many scholars see drought, on top of population pressure and endless war, as a main cause of the collapse.

steps.name: Last king of Copán
steps.what: An altar for a would-be king, Ukit Took', was begun at Copan but left unfinished, the last royal monument there.
steps.why: Copan's dynasty of about 400 years ended, though farmers stayed in the valley for some time.

steps.name: Last monument at Tikal
steps.what: Stela 11, Tikal's last dated monument, was set up in the Great Plaza.
steps.why: After this Tikal's population fell steeply and the city was largely abandoned.

steps.name: Rise of Chichen Itza
steps.what: Chichen Itza in northern Yucatan grew into the region's leading city, with new styles of building and wide trade networks.
steps.why: Power shifted north as the southern cities emptied.

steps.name: Toniná Monument 101
steps.what: A monument at Tonina carries the date 10.4.0.0.0, the last known Long Count date in the Maya lowlands.
steps.why: The end of the Long Count calendar on monuments marks the end of classic Maya kingship.
